disclaimer: These notes were written with AI assistance, drawing on standard commentaries. For study only.

zengwanglun.summary: A seven-character quatrain. Li Bai is about to leave by boat when he hears friends singing and stamping out the rhythm on the bank. He then measures the depth of Peach Blossom Pool against Wang Lun's friendship. The comparison is fresh and natural, and the whole poem is plain, warm and unadorned.
zengwanglun.translation:
Li Bai is aboard his boat, about to set off,
When suddenly from the bank comes the sound of stamping song.
Peach Blossom Pool is a thousand feet deep,
Yet it falls short of the feeling with which Wang Lun sees me off.

glossary.note: A folk way of singing: people link arms, beat time by stamping their feet, and sing as they walk along.
A deep green pool in Jing county, in present-day Anhui province.
An exaggeration, meaning that the water is extremely deep.
The depth of the water is used to set off the depth of the friendship: even a pool this deep falls short of it.

zengwanglun.background: By Li Bai, the great poet of the Tang dynasty (618-907). The poem is traditionally said to have been given to Wang Lun, a man of Jing county whom Li Bai befriended on a visit there, as a parting gift.

wanglushanpubu.summary: A seven-character quatrain describing the grandeur of the waterfall on Mount Lu pouring down from a great height. The first two lines show purple mist in the sunlight and the falls seen from afar; the last two use exaggeration and imagination to turn the waterfall into the Milky Way dropping from the ninth heaven.
wanglushanpubu.translation:
Sunlight strikes Incense Burner Peak and purple mist rises;
From afar the waterfall hangs before the river valley.
Flying, it rushes straight down, three thousand feet,
As if the Silver River were falling from the ninth heaven.

glossary.note: The Incense Burner Peak of Mount Lu. It is named for the clouds and mist that curl around it like smoke rising from an incense burner.
Mist that looks purple when sunlight shines through the water vapour.
The river or mountain stream in front of the viewer. One version of the text reads 「長川」 (a long river).
The ancients believed that Heaven had nine layers. The 'ninth heaven' means the very highest part of the sky.
An exaggeration, meaning that the waterfall is extremely tall.

wanglushanpubu.background: By Li Bai, one of his famous poems, written on a visit to Mount Lu.

gulangyuexing.summary: A five-character poem in the old yuefu (ballad) manner. It begins with the legends of the moon and a child's innocent picture of it, then turns to an eclipse and contrasts it with the old myth of Hou Yi shooting down the suns. The poet laments that the moon is being eaten away and the world thrown into disorder, and ends in anguish. It is commonly read as a veiled criticism of the court.
gulangyuexing.translation:
As a child I did not know the moon;
I called it a white jade plate.
Then I wondered if it was a mirror from the Jade Terrace,
Flying at the edge of the blue clouds.
An immortal lets his two feet hang down,
And the cassia tree grows round and full.
The white hare has pounded the medicine; it is done.
I ask: for whom is it meant to eat?
The toad is eating away the round shadow,
And the great brightness is already ragged in the night.
In the old days Yi shot down nine of the sun-crows,
And Heaven and the human world were clear and calm.
Now the essence of yin sinks into confusion;
Go, go; it is not worth looking at.
Sorrow comes. What can I do?
Grief and anguish break my heart and liver.

glossary.note: In legend, the jade towers where the immortals live.
Legend says a white hare on the moon pounds the elixir of immortality. The character used here is a variant of the usual 「搗」.

glossary.en: chan chu shi yuan ying - 'the toad eats the round shadow'
glossary.note: Legend says a toad lives on the moon, so a lunar eclipse looked as if the toad were swallowing it.

glossary.en: Yi xi luo jiu wu - 'Yi once shot down nine crows'
glossary.note: The myth of Hou Yi, the archer who shot down nine of the ten suns. The 'crow' is the three-legged crow that lives in the sun.
A name for the moon. The ancients counted the moon as yin (the dark, feminine principle), so called it the essence of yin.
Literally 'going further and further away'. Here it carries the sense of 'enough, never mind'.

gulangyuexing.background: By Li Bai. The title borrows the old yuefu title 'Song of the Bright Moon' and adds 'Ancient' (the character 「古」) to show that the poem imitates the old style.

qingpingdiaoqiyi.summary: A seven-character quatrain, the first of three 'Qingping Melodies'. Clouds and flowers stand for the clothes and face of Yang Guifei, spring wind and dew add to her radiance, and in the last line she is likened to a figure from the paradise of the immortals.
qingpingdiaoqiyi.translation:
Clouds make one think of her robes, flowers of her face;
The spring breeze brushes the railing, and the dew shines thick.
If one did not see her on the peak of Mount Qunyu,
One would surely meet her under the moon at the Jade Terrace.

glossary.en: yun xiang yi shang hua xiang rong - 'clouds make one think of her robes, flowers of her face'
glossary.note: Two readings are possible: seeing clouds makes one think of her robes and seeing flowers makes one think of her face; or her robes are like the clouds and her face like the flowers.
A railing or balustrade.
The glitter of dew. The dew makes the colour of the flowers look fresher and brighter.
In legend, the fairy mountain where the Queen Mother of the West lives.
The jade terrace where the immortals live.

qingpingdiaoqiyi.background: Li Bai wrote these poems on the command of Emperor Xuanzong. Tradition says the emperor and Yang Guifei, his favourite consort, were admiring tree peonies in the Aloeswood Pavilion and called Li Bai in to write new lyrics for the occasion.

qingpingdiaoqier.summary: A seven-character quatrain, the second of the 'Qingping Melodies'. A red peony heavy with dew stands for the consort. The story of the goddess of Wu Mountain is brought in as a foil: even the king of Chu's dream goddess could only break his heart in vain. The poem ends by asking who in the Han palace could compare, and only Zhao Feiyan in fresh make-up comes close.
qingpingdiaoqier.translation:
One branch of red beauty, the dew congealed and fragrant;
The clouds and rain of Wu Mountain broke a heart in vain.
I ask, in the Han palace, who could be like her?
Only Feiyan, lovely, with her make-up newly done.

glossary.en: yi zhi hong yan - 'one branch of red beauty'
glossary.note: Refers to the peony, and also hints at Yang Guifei.

glossary.en: yun yu Wu shan - 'clouds and rain of Wu Mountain'
glossary.note: An allusion to Song Yu's 'Rhapsody on Gaotang', in which the king of Chu dreams of meeting the goddess of Wu Mountain.
To grieve for nothing.
Zhao Feiyan, empress of Emperor Cheng of Han, famous for her slender grace and beauty.
An old sense of the word, 'lovable, endearing'. It does not mean 'pitiful', as it does today.

qingpingdiaoqier.background: The second of the three 'Qingping Melodies', written by Li Bai at the emperor's command like the first and the third.

qingpingdiaoqisan.summary: A seven-character quatrain, the third of the 'Qingping Melodies'. The famous flower and the beauty who could topple a state set each other off, and both make the ruler smile as he watches. The last line closes the scene gracefully with the consort leaning on the railing north of the Aloeswood Pavilion.
qingpingdiaoqisan.translation:
The famous flower and the beauty who could topple a state delight in each other,
And the ruler looks on with a smile, again and again.
They dissolve the spring wind's endless sorrow,
As she leans on the railing north of the Aloeswood Pavilion.

glossary.en: ming hua qing guo - 'famous flower, state-toppling beauty'
glossary.note: The famous flower is the peony; the state-toppling beauty is Yang Guifei. The phrase 'toppling a state' comes from a song by Li Yannian.
To dispel or remove. This is the old meaning; it does not mean 'to explain', as it does now.

glossary.en: chun feng wu xian hen - 'the spring wind's endless sorrow'
glossary.note: The endless melancholy and regret that spring stirs up.
A pavilion in the Xingqing Palace in Chang'an, the Tang capital.
The same as the more usual word for a railing.

wenwangchanglingzuoqianlongbiaoyaoyoucij.summary: A seven-character quatrain. Li Bai hears that his friend Wang Changling has been demoted to a remote post at Longbiao. It is late spring, the willow fluff has all fallen and the cuckoo is calling, and he entrusts his sorrow to the moon, hoping the wind will carry it all the way to his friend.
wenwangchanglingzuoqianlongbiaoyaoyoucij.translation:
The willow fluff has fallen away and the cuckoo cries;
I hear that you are passing the Five Streams on the way to Longbiao.
I send my sorrowing heart to the bright moon,
To go with the wind straight on, west of Yelang.

glossary.note: To be demoted. In ancient times the right side was the place of honour and the left the lower place, so being moved down in rank was called 'moving to the left'.
A place around Qianyang in present-day Hunan. Wang Changling was demoted to be the district defender (a minor military post) of Longbiao.
Willow catkins, the fluff that drifts in late spring.
The cuckoo, whose mournful cry often stirs the wish to go home.
The area of five streams in western Hunan and eastern Guizhou. It stands for a remote and wild region.
An old place name, used here loosely for the far south-west.

wenwangchanglingzuoqianlongbiaoyaoyoucij.background: By Li Bai. Wang Changling was a famous poet of the High Tang. When he was sent down to Longbiao, Li Bai wrote this poem to comfort him.

yesushansi.summary: A five-character quatrain. Staying overnight in a very tall building at a mountain temple, the poet feels he could reach out and pick the stars, yet dares not speak loudly for fear of waking the people of Heaven. The exaggeration and imagination show the height, and the language is childlike and innocent.
yesushansi.translation:
The tall tower is a hundred feet high;
One could reach out and pluck the stars.
I dare not speak in a loud voice,
For fear of startling the people in Heaven.

glossary.note: A high building. Here 「危」 means 'high'.
A way of saying it is extremely high, not an exact number.
A general word for the stars.
The immortals in the sky.

yueye.summary: A five-character regulated poem. Trapped in Chang'an, the poet imagines his wife in Fuzhou watching the moon alone, and thinks of his young children, who are too small to know what it is to miss their father. The poem never says that he is homesick; it says that his family misses him, which makes the feeling deeper and more roundabout.
yueye.translation:
Tonight the moon over Fuzhou -
In her chamber she watches it alone.
From far away I pity my small children,
Who cannot yet understand longing for Chang'an.
Fragrant mist dampens her cloud-like coils of hair;
In the clear light her jade-white arms are cold.
When shall we lean by the sheer curtain,
Both lit by the moon, our tear-stains dry?

glossary.note: A place in present-day Fu county, Shaanxi, where Du Fu's wife and children had taken refuge.
The inner room where his wife stays.
Young children.
A thick coil of hair, like a cloud.
A thin curtain that lets light through.
The moonlight shines on husband and wife together.

yueye.background: By Du Fu, written during the An Lushan Rebellion, around 756, while he was held in Chang'an by the rebel army.

chunyexiyu.summary: A five-character regulated poem on the joy of timely spring rain at night. The first four lines praise the rain that knows its season and moistens things without a sound; the last four describe the river scene on a rainy night and imagine the flowers of Chengdu heavy with rain the next morning.
chunyexiyu.translation:
Good rain seems to know its season;
It falls just when spring brings things to life.
It follows the wind and steals in by night,
Moistening all things, fine and without a sound.
The field paths and the clouds are black together;
On the river, only the light of a boat is bright.
At dawn I will see the wet red places:
The flowers will hang heavy in the Brocade City.

glossary.note: To burst into growth. This is the old meaning; it does not mean 'to happen', as it does today.
To soak and nourish all living things.
A small path through the fields.

glossary.en: hong shi chu - 'the wet red places'
glossary.note: The patches of red flowers soaked by the rain.
The flowers look heavy and full because they hold the rain.
Another name for Chengdu.

chunyexiyu.background: By Du Fu, written at his thatched cottage in Chengdu, in the spring of about 761.

zenghuaqing.summary: A seven-character quatrain. On the surface it praises music so fine that it should belong only to Heaven and is rarely heard among people. Some read a gentle satire behind it: that officers of the general Hua Jingding were presuming to use music reserved for the emperor, so the words can be taken two ways.

glossary.note: Hua Jingding, a general in Chengdu. 'Qing' is a respectful form of address for him.
Another name for Chengdu, also called the Brocade Officials' City.
String and wind instruments, meaning music in general.
Describes the sound of music as plentiful, mixed and drifting about.
The same as the common word meaning 'should only'. The first character is a variant of 「祇」.

zenghuaqing.background: By Du Fu, written in Chengdu. Hua Jingding had helped put down a rebellion, but he is said to have had poor discipline among his troops and to have been arrogant, which is why some readers find a hint of mockery here.

shizhisaishang.summary: A five-character regulated poem on the journey and sights of an official mission to the frontier. The first four lines show a lone traveller drifting like tumbleweed and a homeward wild goose; the third couplet, 'In the great desert a lone column of smoke rises straight; over the long river the setting sun is round', paints the vast scenery beyond the wall. The last couplet tells of meeting scout riders and learning that the commander is at the front.
shizhisaishang.translation:
A single light carriage, going to ask after the frontier,
I pass the vassal lands and go by Juyan.
Like a wandering tumbleweed I leave the Han passes;
Like a returning wild goose I enter the sky of the Hu.
In the great desert one lone column of smoke stands straight;
Over the long river the setting sun is round.
At Xiao Pass I meet the mounted scouts:
The Protector-General is at Yanran.

glossary.note: Short for the Han office of 'Director of Dependent States'. Here it means the tribes that had submitted to the empire, or the envoy's own name for himself.
A place name, around Ejin Banner in present-day Inner Mongolia.
Tumbleweed that rolls about with the wind, a figure for a wandering life.
Cavalry who scout and carry reports.
The military and civil governor who guarded the frontier.
Mount Yanran, today's Hangai Mountains in Mongolia. Here it stands loosely for the front line.

shizhisaishang.background: By Wang Wei. Around 737 he was sent to Hexi, in the north-west, to comfort the frontier army, and he wrote this poem on the way.

guanlie.summary: A five-character regulated poem about a general hunting. It opens with a strong wind and the twang of the horn bow; the middle couplets show the swift chase and the return to camp; and the last couplet looks back at the place where the eagle was shot, with evening clouds lying flat for a thousand li, ending in a wide, far-reaching view.
guanlie.translation:
The wind is fierce and the horn bow sings;
The general hunts at Weicheng.
The grass is withered, so the hawk's eye is quick;
The snow is gone, so the horse's hooves are light.
Suddenly he passes the market of Xinfeng,
And is back again at the camp of Thin Willows.
Looking back to where he shot the eagle,
Evening clouds lie flat for a thousand li.

glossary.note: A strong bow decorated with animal horn.
The old site of Xianyang, the capital of Qin, near present-day Xianyang in Shaanxi.
A market town near Chang'an in Tang times, north-east of present-day Lintong in Shaanxi.
The camp where the Han general Zhou Yafu stationed his troops. It was famous for strict discipline and lay south-west of present-day Xianyang. Here it means the general's own camp.
To bring down a great eagle, a sign of superb archery.

niaomingjian.summary: A five-character quatrain, one of a group of poems on Huangfu Yue's Cloud Stream. It paints the stillness of a spring night in the mountains: osmanthus blossom falls without a sound, and the rising moon startles the birds. Using sound to show silence, it is empty and far away in feeling.

glossary.note: A person whose mind is quiet and unhurried. The character used is a variant of 「閒」, the usual word for 'leisure'.
Here it means the spring osmanthus, whose small light flowers fall almost without sound.

glossary.en: chun shan kong - 'the spring mountain empty'
glossary.note: The mountain on a spring night is wide, empty and silent.
A mountain stream in spring.

niaomingjian.background: By Wang Wei, from his set of five poems on Huangfu Yue's Cloud Stream. Huangfu Yue was a friend of his.

zhongnanbieye.summary: A five-character regulated poem on Wang Wei's easy life in his later years in retirement in the Zhongnan Mountains: going out alone for pleasure, sitting to watch the clouds rise when the stream runs out, and chatting with an old man of the woods until he forgets to go home. 'Walking to where the water ends, sitting to watch the time the clouds arise' has become a famous line about going along with things.
zhongnanbieye.translation:
In middle age I came to love the Way;
In later years I made my home at the foot of the southern mountains.
When the mood comes I always go out alone;
The fine things of it I alone know.
I walk until I reach where the water ends,
Then sit and watch the time the clouds arise.
By chance I meet an old man of the woods,
And we talk and laugh with no time set for going back.

glossary.note: Middle age.
To love the teachings of Buddhism and Daoism. In Tang usage this mostly means those ideas.

glossary.en: Nan shan chui - 'edge of the southern mountains'
glossary.note: The foot of the Zhongnan Mountains. The word for 'edge' means a boundary or fringe.
Things that are beautiful or give deep pleasure.

glossary.en: lin sou - 'old man of the woods'
glossary.note: An old man who lives in the mountain woods.

glossary.en: wu huan qi - 'no time to return'
glossary.note: There is no fixed time at which he has to go home.

zhongnanbieye.background: By Wang Wei, written in his later years, when he was half in office and half in retirement, living in the Zhongnan Mountains and at Wangchuan.

liangzhouci.summary: A seven-character quatrain on the bleakness of the frontier and the homesickness of the soldiers who guard it. The first two lines show the Yellow River climbing far into the white clouds and a lone fort under towering mountains. The last two use the flute tune 'Breaking the Willow' to say that the spring wind never reaches Jade Gate Pass, hinting at the guards' sorrow without stating it.
liangzhouci.translation:
The Yellow River climbs far away into the white clouds;
A lone city stands among mountains ten thousand ren high.
Why should the Qiang flute bemoan the willows?
The spring wind never crosses Jade Gate Pass.

glossary.en: Huang He yuan shang bai yun jian - 'the Yellow River climbs far into the white clouds'
glossary.note: One version has 'yellow sand' for 'Yellow River'. Both texts have been handed down.
An old unit of length of seven or eight chi (feet). 'Ten thousand ren' means extremely high.
A wind instrument of the Qiang people of the west.
Refers to the tune 'Breaking the Willow', whose words are mostly about parting.
An important pass on the Han road to the Western Regions, north-west of present-day Dunhuang in Gansu.

liangzhouci.background: By Wang Zhihuan, one of the best-known frontier poems of the High Tang.

yongliu.summary: A seven-character quatrain on the willow in early spring. The first two lines make the tree a beauty dressed in green jade, with branches hanging like silk ribbons. The last two ask who cut the fine leaves, and answer that the spring wind of the second month is like a pair of scissors. The comparison is fresh and lively.
yongliu.translation:
A tree, dressed in green jade, stands tall;
Ten thousand branches hang down like green silk ribbons.
I do not know who cut out these fine leaves -
The spring wind of the second month is like a pair of scissors.

glossary.note: Green jade, used for the deep green of the willow.
Finished dressing and making up. It turns the willow into a beauty.
A silk ribbon, a figure for the willow branches. The last character is a variant of 「絛」.
To cut cloth to shape.
The second month of the lunar calendar, the beginning of spring.

yongliu.background: By He Zhizhang, a well-known Tang poem in the genre that describes a single object.

dengkehou.summary: A seven-character quatrain on the joy of passing the imperial examination. The cramped hardship of the past is set against today's triumph, and the galloping hooves and 'seeing all the flowers of Chang'an in a day' show how delighted he is. The feeling is open and frank.

glossary.note: To pass the imperial civil service examination. Here it means winning the jinshi degree, the highest level.
Narrow and confined, describing the poor and frustrated days of the past. This is the old meaning and has nothing to do with today's sense of 'dirty'.
Unrestrained and expansive. In the old usage the word has no bad sense.
Without edge or limit.

glossary.en: Chang An hua - 'the flowers of Chang'an'
glossary.note: The spring flowers of the capital, Chang'an. It also carries the sense of the new jinshi graduates touring and enjoying them.

dengkehou.background: By Meng Jiao, who failed the examination again and again and only passed the jinshi at about the age of forty-six.

minnong.summary: A five-character quatrain. A farmer hoes his field under the midday sun, sweat dripping into the soil, and the poet reminds us that every grain of rice on the plate was won by hard labour. It is a plea not to waste food.
minnong.translation:
Hoeing the millet under the noonday sun,
sweat drips down into the soil beneath the crop.
Who knows that the food upon the plate,
grain after grain, is all hard toil?

glossary.note: To weed and loosen the soil around the young plants.

glossary.en: ri dang wu - 'the sun is at noon'
glossary.note: The sun stands right overhead, so it is midday, the hottest time of the day.

glossary.en: pan zhong sun - 'cooked food on the plate'
glossary.note: The meal on the plate. The rare character for 'sun' here means cooked food or cooked grain.
Bitter labour and difficulty.

minnong.background: By Li Shen, a Tang dynasty (618-907) poet. It is the second of his two poems titled 'Pity the Farmers'.

fudeguyuancaosongbie.summary: A five-character regulated poem, written on the set theme of grass on an ancient plain, as a farewell. The first four lines show grass withering and returning with stubborn life; the last four spread the fragrant grass along old roads and ruined walls, and from its lushness arise the sorrow and reluctance of parting from a friend.
fudeguyuancaosongbie.translation:
Thick and lush, the grass upon the plain:
every year it withers, and every year it thrives.
Wildfire cannot burn it all away;
when the spring wind blows, it grows again.
Far-off fragrance creeps over the old road,
sunlit green runs up to the ruined city wall.
Once more I see my noble friend depart,
and the thick grass is full of parting feeling.

glossary.en: fu de - 'composing on a given theme'
glossary.note: A title formula meaning a poem written on an assigned subject, as in an exercise or at a gathering. The title begins with it.
Describes grass growing dense and abundant.
The grass dies back and then thrives again, a yearly cycle.
Originally a descendant of nobles. Here it means the friend who is leaving.
Describes grass growing richly. The lushness of the grass becomes a picture of how full the parting feeling is.

fudeguyuancaosongbie.background: By Bai Juyi (772-846), one of the great Tang poets. It is said to be an exercise from his youth, and it later became one of his most famous poems.

dalinsitaohua.summary: A seven-character quatrain. In early summer the poet climbs a high mountain and unexpectedly finds peach blossom in full bloom at Dalin Temple. He treats spring as a guest who has slipped away into the mountains, and the tone is delighted and playful, full of love for the season.
dalinsitaohua.translation:
In the world below, April's blossoms are all gone,
but at the mountain temple the peach flowers are only now in full bloom.
I have long regretted that spring left and could not be found,
never knowing it had turned and come in here.

glossary.note: Here it means the ordinary world down on the plain, in contrast to the high mountain.
Flowers and grasses in full, sweet-smelling bloom.
An old temple, dating from the Jin dynasty (265-420), near the top of Censer Peak on Mount Lu.
To look for something.
To have felt regret again and again.

dalinsitaohua.background: By Bai Juyi, written around 817 when he toured Mount Lu in Jiangxi.

qiantanghuchunxing.summary: A seven-character regulated poem about an early-spring walk around West Lake at Hangzhou. It lists fresh sights: early orioles, new swallows carrying mud, scattered blossom and short grass. The closing couplet names his favourite spot, the white sand causeway under green willows. The mood is light and clear.
qiantanghuchunxing.translation:
North of Gushan Temple, west of Jia Pavilion,
the lake is just level with its banks and the clouds hang low.
Here and there early orioles squabble over sunny trees;
whose house do the new swallows belong to, pecking at spring mud?
A riot of flowers is beginning to dazzle the eye,
the shallow grass is only deep enough to hide a horse's hooves.
What I love best is the east of the lake, where I can never walk enough,
the white sand causeway in the shade of green willows.

glossary.note: Another name for West Lake in Hangzhou.
A temple on Solitary Hill, an island in West Lake.
A pavilion built by Jia Quan, a Tang governor of Hangzhou; it is also called Jia Gong Pavilion.

glossary.en: shui mian chu ping - 'the water has just risen level'
glossary.note: The lake has just risen to the height of the embankment.
Refers to the White Causeway across West Lake.
No amount of walking is enough; he is never satisfied.

qiantanghuchunxing.background: By Bai Juyi, written in the Changqing era (821-824) when he served as prefect of Hangzhou.

chishang.summary: A five-character regulated poem on a pond in early autumn. Cool wind stirs, cold dew drips, orchids fade and lotus leaves tear. Only a lone crane and a pair of fireflies keep company. The closing couplet ties this lonely scene to the poet sobering up from wine, and leaves a quiet autumn solitude.

glossary.note: Describes soft, gently moving wind. It is the same word as another character with the same sound and meaning.
A cold, desolate feeling.
To drop; here the dew drops fall.

glossary.en: qi sha he - 'a crane roosting on the sand'
glossary.note: A crane resting on a sandbank in the pond.
A hard phrase. It can be read as 'how could one bear' or simply 'such'. Commentators differ a little; here it points to the lonely scene.
Quiet, deserted and forlorn.

yijiangnan.summary: A set of three song lyrics (ci) to the tune 'Remembering Jiangnan', written by Bai Juyi in old age. The first song praises the scenery of Jiangnan, the south of the Yangtze, in general; the other two recall moon-gazing at a mountain temple and watching the tidal bore in Hangzhou, then the fine wine and beautiful women of Suzhou. The language is fresh and the feeling sincere.
yijiangnan.translation:
Jiangnan is lovely;
its scenery I once knew well.
When the sun comes up, the river flowers are redder than fire;
when spring arrives, the river water is green as indigo.
How could I not remember Jiangnan?
I remember Jiangnan,
and most of all I remember Hangzhou.
In the mountain temple on a moonlit night, I looked for cassia seeds;
in the prefecture pavilion, I watched the crest of the tide from my pillow.
When shall I visit it again?
I remember Jiangnan,
and next I remember the palace of Wu.
A cup of Wu wine, bamboo-leaf green in spring;
Wu girls dancing in pairs, drunk like lotus flowers.
Sooner or later, shall we meet again?

glossary.note: To be familiar with something.
The blue-dye plant, indigo. Its deep blue-green colour is used to describe the river water in spring.
In legend, on Mid-Autumn night seeds of the moon's cassia tree fall around Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou.
Means Suzhou, which was the capital of the state of Wu in the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BC).
Bamboo-leaf green, a famous clear green wine.
A beautiful young woman of the Wu region.

yijiangnan.background: Written by Bai Juyi in his later years while living in Luoyang, looking back on Hangzhou and Suzhou, where he had once served as prefect.

xiaoerchuidiao.summary: A seven-character quatrain describing a scruffy little boy learning to fish among the grass. He sits very still, and when a passer-by asks the way he waves from a distance, not daring to answer for fear of frightening the fish. It is innocent and full of fun.
xiaoerchuidiao.translation:
A tousle-headed child is learning to fish,
sitting sideways on the mossy bank, hidden by the grass.
A passer-by calls out to ask the way; he waves from afar,
afraid the fish will be startled, he does not answer.

glossary.note: Hair loose, messy and untidy.
A small child.

glossary.en: chui lun - 'to lower a fishing line'
glossary.note: To let down the fishing line, that is, to fish. The second character means the silk line used in fishing.
Green moss growing on the ground.
A polite way of asking someone for information, such as the way.

xiaoerchuidiao.background: By Hu Lingneng, a Tang poet about whom almost nothing is known.

xinggong.summary: A five-character quatrain. In a lonely old travelling palace the palace flowers still bloom red, and white-haired palace women sit idly talking about Emperor Xuanzong. A lonely scene sets off the changes of human life, and in twenty characters it carries a sense of rise and fall, flourishing and decay.
xinggong.translation:
Deserted and desolate, the old travelling palace;
the palace flowers bloom red in solitude.
White-haired palace women are still there,
sitting idly, talking of Xuanzong.

glossary.note: A secondary palace where an emperor stayed while on a journey.
Deserted, cold and run-down.
Flowers growing in the palace grounds.
Li Longji, the Tang emperor who reigned 712-756. His reign saw the height of the dynasty and then the An Lushan Rebellion, which began its decline.

xinggong.background: By Yuan Zhen, a friend of Bai Juyi. The poem is set in a travelling palace after the An Lushan Rebellion (755-763) and is usually read as carrying a sense of the rise and fall of dynasties.

shanxing.summary: A seven-character quatrain about a walk in the mountains in autumn: a winding stone path, a few homes where white clouds rise, and the poet halting his carriage to admire the maples at dusk. Frost-reddened leaves seem redder than spring flowers. It breaks with the usual sad tone of autumn poems and is bright and clear.
shanxing.translation:
Far up the cold mountain, a stone path slants;
where white clouds rise, there are people's homes.
I stop my carriage because I love the maple woods at dusk,
frost-touched leaves redder than flowers in the second month.

glossary.note: A mountain deep in late autumn, heavy with chill.
A path paved with stones.
Sloping or slanted. In old poetry it is also read xia, to fit the rhyme.
In old Chinese this word means 'because', not 'to sit'.
Maple leaves that have turned red after frost.

shanxing.background: By Du Mu (803-852), a late Tang poet. It is one of the best-known poems on autumn scenery.

shangshanzaoxing.summary: A five-character regulated poem about a traveller setting out at dawn. He hurries along under cockcrow, a fading moon and a frosted plank bridge; then come fallen leaves on the mountain road and bright orange blossom by the wall of a post station. Moved by the scene, he ends with a dream of his home at Duling, its ponds full of wild ducks and geese.
shangshanzaoxing.translation:
Rising at dawn, the travelling bells begin to ring;
the wanderer, setting out, grieves for his old home.
A cock crows, a thatched inn, the moon;
footprints on a plank bridge, the frost.
Oak leaves fall on the mountain road,
orange blossom brightens the wall of the post station.
And so I think of my dream of Duling:
wild ducks and geese filling the winding pond.

glossary.note: The bells hung on carts and horses that go on a long journey.
A simple country inn roofed with thatch.
A tall deciduous tree with large, thick leaves that fall in autumn and winter.
The flower of the trifoliate orange tree, which bears small white blossoms in spring.
A place south-east of the capital Chang'an, where the poet once lived. Here it stands for his home.
A pond with a curving shore.

shangshanzaoxing.background: By Wen Tingyun, a late Tang poet (Tang dynasty, 618-907). Shangshan is in today's Shangluo in Shaanxi, a place he passed on a journey, whether on the way to a post or away from the capital.

yanmentaishouxing.summary: A seven-character yuefu poem about a frontier garrison besieged by a huge enemy army: black clouds pressing on the city, armour glinting, horns sounding, and soldiers still fighting through heavy frost and cold nights. It ends with a vow to repay the ruler's trust with their lives. The colours are intense and the mood is tragic and heroic.
yanmentaishouxing.translation:
Black clouds press on the city, the city is about to be crushed;
in the sun the glint of armour opens like golden scales.
Horn calls fill the sky in the colours of autumn;
beyond the frontier the rouge-red blood congeals into night purple.
With red banners half furled we reach the River Yi,
the frost is heavy, the drums are cold and give no sound.
To repay the lord for the favour of the Terrace of Gold,
we take up our jade-dragon swords and will die for him.

glossary.en: Yanmen taishou xing - 'Ballad of the Governor of Yanmen'
glossary.note: An old yuefu (folk-song style) title that once told of a governor of Yanmen. Li He borrows it to write about a battle on the frontier.
Golden fish scales, a picture of armour flashing in the sunlight.
A red-purple cosmetic. Here it describes the dark purple-red of blood.
A river in today's Hebei, where Jing Ke was seen off before his attempt to kill the future First Emperor of Qin.
According to tradition, King Zhao of Yan built a terrace and put gold on it to attract wise men to his service.
A fine name for a precious sword.

yanmentaishouxing.background: By Li He (790-816), one of his most famous poems, known for its strange and brilliant style.

fengxuesufurongshanzhuren.summary: A five-character quatrain about a snowy night. At dusk the hills look far away and the sky is cold; a poor thatched hut stands there, and suddenly dogs bark at the wattle gate: someone is coming home through wind and snow. The picture is plain and warm, and the last line is especially vivid.
fengxuesufurongshanzhuren.translation:
At sunset the green hills seem far away;
in the cold sky the bare white cottage looks poor.
At the brushwood gate I hear a dog bark:
someone coming home through wind and snow at night.

glossary.note: Evening, when the sun is going down.
Hills in deep blue-green.
A plain house of ordinary people, with no paint or decoration; in other words, a thatched cottage.
A place name. Its exact location is disputed.

fengxuesufurongshanzhuren.background: By Liu Changqing, a Tang poet. Readers have long disagreed whether the person who returns is the poet, a guest seeking a night's shelter, or the host of the house.

yuweng.summary: A six-line old-style poem about an old fisherman. He moors by the west cliff for the night, then draws clear river water and burns bamboo at dawn. When the mist clears there is only the creak of an oar and the hills and water turn green; his boat drifts downstream, and idle clouds follow over the cliff. The mood is open and detached, expressing the poet's lofty, aloof heart.

glossary.note: To draw near to something, here the cliff.
A major river in Hunan, near where the poet lived in exile.
Bamboo from the old land of Chu, the region of the middle Yangtze, including Hunan.
The sound of an oar being rowed, or, some say, a fisherman's song. It is read ai nai.
The poet Tao Yuanming wrote of clouds that drift out of the peaks without any intention. Liu Zongyuan borrows the free clouds to suggest the pleasure of a hermit's life.

yuweng.background: By Liu Zongyuan (773-819), written while he was demoted and living in Yongzhou.

jiangshangyuzhe.summary: A five-character quatrain. Travellers going to and fro on the river think only of how delicious perch tastes, and hardly of the fishermen risking their lives in the waves. In few words, by contrast, it stirs sympathy and thought.
jiangshangyuzhe.translation:
The people coming and going on the river
all love the fine taste of perch.
Just look at that boat, small as a leaf,
appearing and vanishing among wind and waves.

glossary.note: A fish of rivers and lakes with delicious flesh, famous in the old Wu region, and highly prized.

glossary.en: yi ye zhou - 'a leaf of a boat'
glossary.note: A tiny boat, as small as a single leaf.
Now showing, now hidden, as the boat rises and falls with the waves.
Rough water whipped up by the wind.

jiangshangyuzhe.background: By Fan Zhongyan, a Song dynasty (960-1279) statesman who cared about ordinary people's lives. This short poem shows his concern for them.

yonge.summary: A widely known short poem on an object, said to have been written when Luo Binwang was seven. The three opening cries of 'goose' imitate the bird's honk; the last two lines use white feathers, green water, red feet and clear ripples to make a vivid colour picture, simple but lively.
yonge.translation:
Goose, goose, goose,
bending its neck towards the sky to sing.
White feathers float on green water,
red feet push through the clear waves.

glossary.note: A bent neck. The second character means the neck.

glossary.en: xiang tian ge - 'sings towards the sky'
glossary.note: Calls out with its head raised to the sky.
The goose's red webbed feet.
To paddle or stir the water.

yonge.background: By Luo Binwang, one of the 'Four Eminent Poets of the Early Tang'. Tradition says he wrote it at the age of seven.

tixilinbi.summary: A seven-character quatrain in which a sightseeing trip on Mount Lu leads to a thought about life: one mountain looks different from every angle, and someone standing inside it cannot see the whole. The poem carries the lesson that to judge well one must step beyond one's own limited position and look at the whole picture.
tixilinbi.translation:
Seen from the side it is a range, from the end a peak;
far or near, high or low, it is never the same.
The true face of Mount Lu I cannot recognise,
only because I am here, inside the mountain.

glossary.note: A temple on Mount Lu.
A long chain of hills.
A steep, standing summit.
How a thing really looks.
It means 'just because'. The first character is an older form of the character for 'only'.

tixilinbi.background: By Su Shi (Su Dongpo, 1037-1101), a Song poet. He wrote it on the wall of Xilin Temple around 1084, when he left Huangzhou for Ruzhou and passed Mount Lu.

yinhushangchuqinghouyu.summary: A seven-character quatrain. West Lake has its own beauty in fine weather, with sparkling water, and in rain, with hazy hills. Then the poet compares the lake to the beauty Xi Shi, who looks right in light make-up or heavy. The fresh comparison made the name 'Xizi Lake' well known.
yinhushangchuqinghouyu.translation:
Rippling light on the water is lovely when the sky clears;
hills in misty haze are strange and fine in the rain.
If I wished to compare West Lake to Xi Shi,
light make-up or heavy, she always suits.

glossary.note: Water shimmering and bright.
Vague and dim, like a veil.
Xi Shi, a famous beauty of the state of Yue in the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BC). The name Xizi means 'Lady Xi'.

glossary.en: dan zhuang nong mo - 'light make-up or heavy'
glossary.note: Light or thick make-up. The first character of 'make-up' in the text is an old variant of the usual one.

yinhushangchuqinghouyu.background: By Su Shi, written around the Xining era (1068-1077), while he was assistant prefect at Hangzhou, at a banquet on West Lake.

huichongchunjiangwanjing.summary: A poem written on a painting, a seven-character quatrain, for Hui Chong's picture 'Spring River at Dusk'. From the bamboo, peach blossom, ducks, artemisia and reed shoots in the picture, the poet imagines the warmth of the spring water, and even the season when puffer fish come upriver. The picture has flavour and the poem is full of charm.
huichongchunjiangwanjing.translation:
Beyond the bamboo, two or three sprays of peach blossom;
the spring river is warm, and the ducks are first to know.
The ground is covered with artemisia, the reed shoots are still short:
it is just the time when the puffer fish want to swim upstream.

glossary.note: A monk of the Northern Song who was good at painting small landscapes.
A wild plant that can be eaten, growing by the water.
The tender young shoot of a reed.
A fish with delicious flesh, but its inner organs are poisonous.

glossary.en: yu shang - 'to want to go upstream'
glossary.note: To swim up against the current. Each spring puffer fish move from the sea into rivers.

huichongchunjiangwanjing.background: By Su Shi, who wrote it on a painting by his friend Hui Chong.
